subject: Career
title: Reading the Interviewer's Signals
description: A quick win: understand Reading the Interviewer's Signals.

hook.text: They started selling you on the role. They mentioned next steps unprompted. These are buying signals.

buildup.text: When interviewers shift from evaluating to selling, they've mentally moved you forward.

discovery.text: Watch for: 'You'd be working with…' or 'When you start…' — future tense is a green light.

twist.text: But don't relax too early. Some interviewers sell to everyone. Only an offer is an offer.

climax.text: When you see buying signals, lean in. Ask about the team, the roadmap, the vision.

punchline.text: When they start selling, you've already won the evaluation.

quiz.question: What is a 'buying signal' from an interviewer?
options: Using future tense about you in the role

details.summary: Interviewers reveal their level of interest through micro-signals like leaning forward, asking follow-up questions, taking notes, and extending the conversation. Learning to read these cues helps you adjust your strategy in real time.
details.whyItMatters: Real-time feedback from interviewer signals lets you double down on topics that resonate and pivot away from areas where you are losing engagement.
takeaways: Note-taking usually indicates the interviewer found your answer noteworthy
Leaning back and checking the clock are disengagement warning signs
Follow-up questions signal genuine curiosity about your experience

faq.question: What is the clearest positive signal an interviewer can give during the conversation?
faq.answer: Selling you on the role or team is the strongest positive signal. When an interviewer shifts from evaluating to persuading, they have likely decided you are a strong candidate and are now trying to ensure you accept an offer.

faq.question: How should you respond if you notice the interviewer seems disengaged?
faq.answer: Shorten your current answer, then re-engage by asking a question about their experience at the company. Shifting the dynamic to a conversation rather than a monologue often reactivates interest and gives you new information to work with.
